observations.statement: The object of interest is the magnitude of inefficient adoption delay (excess inertia), quantified as differences in aggregate theatre surplus between the market equilibrium and two counterfactual planner benchmarks; the design is a dynamic game of technology adoption estimated with CCP methods under a non-stationary oblivious equilibrium.

Identification is discussed in a dedicated subsection: the econometrician observes a single large population of firms playing one equilibrium over a finite horizon, so parameters come from many firms of the same type in one market and the multiple equilibria issue is sidestepped rather than assumed away across markets.
observations.quote: By using only a single market, the article sidesteps the multiplicity issue

observations.statement: Formal numbered assumptions structure the argument: oblivious strategies (Assumption 1), data generated by a NOE that becomes stationary (Assumption 2), and payoff normalizations for the film technology and for zero digital availability (Assumption 3), with a counting argument for exact versus over identification and a lemma proved in the supplementary appendix.

Endogeneity of digital movie availability is handled in two steps following Gowrisankaran, Park and Rysman: time dummies replace availability in the profit decay, then the dummy coefficients are regressed on availability instrumented by the US digital release share; exclusion rests on US release decisions not depending on the French installed base.

A footnote flags that the instrument would be weaker if common aggregate shocks affected both countries, and argues the payoff normalization differences out aggregate box office shocks independent of format.
Standard conventions of the dynamic discrete choice literature are invoked explicitly: the discount factor and the shock distribution are assumed known, with citations to identification papers.

The main panel of screen-level digital adoption is assembled from two public sources (industry yearbooks and an online database accessed via the Internet Archive), observed at irregular snapshot dates; three auxiliary datasets (national film agency, European Audiovisual Observatory cost series, IMDb release formats) are described with their coverage periods.
Snapshot dates are pruned to make the panel approximately semi-annual, with the procedure relegated to the online appendix; the panel stops before diffusion is complete.

Exclusions are listed one by one with a reason each: itinerant theatres, entrants already digital (kept only as exogenous installed base), exiters before conversion, overseas territories; entry and exit rates are cited as low to justify treating the firm set as fixed.

The estimation sample is further restricted to theatres with at least four screens because smaller theatres received government subsidies allocated on an administrative timeline, so their adoption is argued not to reflect an optimization problem; the resulting counts of theatres and markets are reported.

Local markets are defined using the national statistics office urban unit definition, with arrondissements substituted in the three largest cities; a footnote reports that distance bands give similar competitor counts as a robustness check.

The adoption cost series is built from a manufacturer survey list price net of the VPF subsidy plus ancillary costs observed only in one year and assumed constant, expressed in constant euros and interpolated to observation dates; the authors note that actual transaction prices are confidential.

The choice variable is the number (or share) of a theatre's screens converted in a period; the state is the stock of digital screens; theatre type bundles size, market size, competitor screens, art house label and chain identity, all fixed over the game.
The instrument is the share of US releases distributed digitally, hand-collected from IMDb technical specifications for all US releases in the period.

The within-theatre adoption share is coarsened onto a grid that differs by theatre size class; the choice is justified with kernel density plots of observed adoption rates and the share of observations near grid points.

The first-stage policy function table shows four ordered probit specifications that progressively add market dummies, chain dummies and size interactions; each column reports estimates with standard errors side by side, observations, negative log likelihood and AIC, and notes name omitted categories.

The structural parameter table reports estimates and bootstrap standard errors, and its notes state the number of bootstrap samples, the omitted categories and the calibrated shock standard deviation.
The preferred first-stage specification is chosen by AIC among the four columns and carried into the second step.

Standard errors for structural parameters use a parametric bootstrap; the authors explain that resampling market or firm histories is invalid here because decisions are correlated across markets and firms, and detail the procedure in the online appendix.
observations.quote: sampling market-histories (or firm-histories) with replacement ... is not a valid approach

observations.statement: For the first-stage ordered probit in Table 3, the standard error type is not described in the text or the table notes.
The two-step time-dummy then IV approach is motivated as addressing hierarchical variation in the manner of Donald and Lang.
A likelihood ratio test comparing the preferred policy function against one including competitors' digital adoption is used to justify modelling strategic interaction only at the industry level.
Model fit of the first-stage policy function (predicted versus actual digital screen shares) is reported in the online appendix and summarized qualitatively in the text.
The finite horizon length is validated by simulating industry trajectories and reporting the share reaching the absorbing steady state by the terminal period.
Reduced-form evidence that gradual adoption is driven by rising digital availability, and a discussion of instrument validity, are placed in the online appendix and referenced from the main text.

Robustness to the discount factor and shock distribution choices, to the chain-independence assumption and to the calibrated reaction function parameters is delegated to the online appendix and mentioned in one sentence each.
observations.locator: Section 6.3, Section 7.1, footnote 32, Supplementary Appendix D.4

observations.statement: The planner benchmark obtained by random search over adoption paths is cross-checked by explicitly solving a reduced-dimension planner problem in the online appendix, and the two are reported as consistent.
A footnote reports that an alternative distance-band market definition yields similar competitor counts.

Heterogeneity in profits per digital screen enters through the parameterization itself (size, art house, competitor screens, market and chain dummies) and is discussed by reading which parameters differ from zero, linked to cost versus revenue channels.
Distributional effects of counterfactual subsidies are reported by theatre size class (mean per-screen subsidy for miniplexes versus multiplexes) and by targeted subsidies to miniplexes only.
Estimated profits per digital screen are benchmarked for plausibility against projectionists' collectively bargained minimum wages over a six-month period, treated as an upper bound on cost savings.

Counterfactual surplus is reported in constant euros and as percentage changes relative to the market outcome, with film profits normalized to zero so all figures are relative to the no-adoption status quo.
Adoption delay is summarized as differences in years to reach fixed adoption milestones across scenarios, plotted as diffusion paths.

The authors note that profits are only identified over the support of the observed availability path and that a cross-section of markets would allow richer identification, motivating the parametric restrictions.
Upstream excess inertia is described as a residual that mixes coordination failure and distributor externalities; the coordination benchmark is argued to be a lower bound on the welfare loss.

Restrictive modelling choices (chains deciding independently, replacing the industry state with its first moment) are flagged with reasons of computational tractability and pointers to appendix discussion.
The introduction and conclusion discuss transfer to other hardware-software industries (USB-C, contactless payments) while noting that which side a planner should target is industry specific.

Two summary statistics tables are provided: one by market size category (counts, means, shares, dispersion) and one with min, mean, max and standard deviation of theatre characteristics and conversion cost.
Tables report estimates and standard errors in adjacent columns without significance stars; significance is discussed verbally in the text.

Descriptive figures show observation dates with the industry adoption share, the cost time series, and a decomposition of new digital screens into extensive and intensive margins; figure notes define the categories and state exclusions.
A table lists every state variable of the model with a description and whether it is observed, estimated or unobserved, to ease navigation.

Counterfactual results are shown as multi-panel diffusion path figures (screens and movies) under benchmarks and subsidy levels, paired with surplus tables that decompose gross profits, adoption costs and net profits.

The introduction previews the main quantitative findings, ends with a roadmap paragraph, and is followed by a separate related literature section organised by strand with explicit points of departure.

Ordering is background, data with descriptive facts that motivate modelling choices, model, estimation and identification, counterfactuals, conclusion; the estimation section is deliberately placed before identification with an explanation of why.

Many procedures (period selection, reduced-form evidence, bootstrap, likelihood construction, fit, planner algorithms, robustness, alternative subsidies) are in a supplementary online appendix not included in the PDF.
Two stylized facts from the data (gradual within-firm rollout, no local strategic interaction) are stated explicitly and each is mapped to a modelling decision.
A data availability statement says data and code are on Zenodo with a DOI, repeated in the supplementary data note.
Main adoption data come from public yearbooks and an archived web database; auxiliary data from a national agency, a European observatory report and IMDb; no restricted access is mentioned.

The decomposition of surplus loss into downstream externalities and upstream coordination failure is produced by nested counterfactuals rather than reduced-form tests; the online appendix checks that mandated multi-homing does not lower distributor profits.
A footnote cites results establishing that subsidy counterfactuals are identified under payoff normalizations because they are pre-specified additive payoff changes.

concordance.paper_says: Two-step CCP estimator: ordered probit policy function then minimum distance on differences in choice-specific value functions, plus a time-dummy IV step
concordance.card_shows: mle2 (bbmle) fit, an lm, and an ivreg 2SLS call; method tagged iv only

concordance.paper_says: First stage CCP estimated by ordered probit
concordance.card_shows: ordinal package listed as unknown usage; no ordered probit spec recorded

concordance.paper_says: Parametric bootstrap with a stated number of replications for structural parameters
No clustering; bootstrap is parametric because market or firm resampling is argued invalid
Theatres with at least four screens, excluding itinerant, overseas, entrants and exiters
Policy function includes time polynomial, own screens, art house, competitor screens, own digital share, market and chain dummies
Time dummy coefficients regressed on digital availability instrumented by US digital share
Media Salles yearbooks, Cinego, CNC, European Audiovisual Observatory, IMDb
Discount factor, shock distribution, reaction function parameters, chain independence, planner solution method (online appendix)

gaps: No standard error type stated for the first-stage ordered probit (Table 3)
No software named in the main text
No balance, placebo or pre-trend diagnostics (not applicable to the design)
Supplementary online appendices A to D are not in the PDF; robustness and bootstrap details could not be read
No preregistration or ethics statement (none expected)
No first-stage strength statistic reported for the US-share instrument in the main text
